newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia promises more reforms, better environment.
newsitem.headline: Serbia promises more reforms, better environment.

text.p: Serbia said on Tuesday it was satisfied with the first quarter economic performance and promised more reforms, but local businesses cited a long list of problems nagging the economy in a year of reforms.
Local company managers called on the government to improve business climate and clear the path to more growth.

Lack of working capital and commercial lending, high interest rates, burgeoning internal debt, a growing trade gap, rising inventories and a massive fiscal burden stood in the way of reaching an ambitious 13 percent GDP growth target in 1997.
"This economy is miserable and it will grow even more so if something is not changed," said Radomir Vujic, general manager of the Cacak-based Sloboda metal-processing factory.

Serbia's economy, almost coming to a halt during three months of opposition street protests over local election fraud which ended in February, recorded a 4.4 percent cumulative year-on-year industry growth in the first two months of 1997.
The growth, coming from a very low base with industries using around 30 percent of their installed capacities, coincided with falling employment.
According to figures released by the Serbian Chamber of Commerce, the number of employed fell to 1.91 million in February and was two percent below the 1996 average.
A senior government official said the first quarter performance was satisfactory in view of planned targets and surroundings.
Serbia declared price and currency stability and improvement in the standards of living as its key 1997 economic policy targets.

"We have maintained price and currency stability. Prices grew by a cumulative three percent in the first three months of 1997, boding well for a fifteen percent annual inflation," Serbian Deputy Prime Minister Svetozar Krstic said.
Krstic insisted the government also kept the dinar stable, despite some problems in December and devaluation expectations.

"Key targets of a stabilisation economic policy are there," he told a gathering at the Serbian Chamber of Commerce and promised the government will do more to create a right climate for a better economic performance.
"We shall adopt a series of reform laws on privatisation, concessions and public enterprises. The government will also do everything to improve relations with the world," Krstic said.
"Right now, lack of relations with the world is the biggest obstacle to the Yugoslav economy. But once it is removed, we shall face another problem -- insufficient quality.
"We shall have to restructure our production and improve quality of our products. Inadequate quality will become our biggest obstacle to return to world markets," he said.

President of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce Vlajko Stojiljkovic called on economic policymakers to do their job, stick to their goals and adopt measures that will lead the whole economy towards proclaimed economic targets.
"There is no reason not to implement those measures."
But Desimir Misic of the Jagodina cable-works regretted the government remained deaf for businesses' needs and proposals.
"Economic policymakers do not accept our suggestions which are free-of-charge, reliable and sincere," he said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
